questions.prompt: A simply supported beam spans 4 m and carries a 600 N point load at midspan. What vertical reaction acts at either support?

feedback.hint: Use symmetry and vertical-force equilibrium.
feedback.solution: The reactions are equal; 2R=600 N, so R=300 N at each support.

questions.prompt: A 50 mm² rod carries 500 N axial tension. What is the average stress in MPa?

feedback.hint: Compute F/A and note 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa.
feedback.solution: σ=500 N/50 mm²=10 N/mm²=10 MPa.

questions.prompt: In elementary beam bending, where is the magnitude of normal stress greatest?
options: At the neutral axis
At the outermost fiber farthest from the neutral axis
Uniformly across the section
Only at a pin support

feedback.hint: Use σ=My/I and ask where |y| is largest.
feedback.solution: Bending stress magnitude is proportional to distance from the neutral axis, so it is greatest at the extreme fibers.

questions.prompt: A part has a specified allowable stress of 120 MPa and a calculated maximum stress of 40 MPa. What is the factor of safety?

feedback.hint: Divide allowable stress by calculated stress.
feedback.solution: FoS=120/40=3 for this stated failure criterion.

questions.prompt: A simply supported beam 4.0 m long carries a single 200 N downward load 1.0 m from the left support. Calculate the reaction at the right support. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Take moments about the left support.
feedback.solution: Moments about the left support: R_right × 4.0 = 200 × 1.0, so R_right = 50 N and R_left = 150 N by force balance.

questions.prompt: A rod carries an axial force of 1200 N over a cross-section of 30 mm². Calculate the axial stress. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Convert mm² to m² or use N/mm², which is MPa.
feedback.solution: σ = 1200 N ÷ 30 mm² = 40 N/mm² = 40 MPa. Unit consistency matters: N/mm² and MPa are the same. A linear stress-strain model applies only below the elastic limit.

questions.prompt: Two bars of equal length 400 mm and area 100 mm² connect the same rigid end plates. Their elastic moduli are 200 GPa and 100 GPa, and the total axial load is 30 kN. What force, in kN, does the 200 GPa bar carry? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Rigid plates impose the same extension; load divides in proportion to axial stiffness AE/L.
feedback.solution: The stiffnesses are 50 and 25 kN/mm, so the 200 GPa bar carries 50/(50+25) × 30 = 20 kN. The two member forces sum to the applied load.

questions.prompt: For the same two-bar assembly, calculate the common end-plate displacement in mm under the 30 kN load. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: The bars act as parallel axial springs with total stiffness 75 kN/mm.
feedback.solution: The common displacement is δ = P/(k₁+k₂) = 30 kN/(75 kN/mm) = 0.4 mm.

questions.prompt: For two axial bars joined by rigid end plates, which relation supplies the compatibility condition needed to resolve their separate member forces?
options: Their axial extensions are equal because both share the same end-plate displacement.
Their internal forces are equal because both carry tension.
Their nominal stresses are equal because their end plates are rigid.
Their extensions sum to zero because the total applied force is balanced.

feedback.hint: Use the geometry of connected displacements, then relate each member's force to its extension.
feedback.solution: The common rigid plates impose equal end displacement and hence equal member extension. Combined with force equilibrium and each bar's elastic force–deformation law, compatibility determines the load share.

questions.prompt: A rectangular beam section (width 0.050 m, depth 0.100 m) carries a bending moment of 500 N·m. Calculate the maximum bending stress σ = M c / I. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: I = b h³/12 and c = h/2.

questions.prompt: A solid circular shaft of diameter 20 mm carries a torque of 10 N·m. Under the elastic circular-shaft model, calculate the maximum shear stress at its outer surface. Enter a value in MPa.

feedback.hint: Use J=πd⁴/32 and τmax=Tc/J. Convert 10 N·m to 10,000 N·mm, or convert the diameter to meters.
feedback.solution: J=π(20 mm)⁴/32=15,708 mm⁴ and c=10 mm. Thus τmax=(10,000 N·mm)(10 mm)/(15,708 mm⁴)=6.37 N/mm²=6.37 MPa.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish common failure criteria? Select all that apply.
options: Yield is the onset of permanent deformation under the stated material condition and test convention.
Ultimate strength is the maximum engineering stress reached on a tensile-test curve.
Fatigue damage can accumulate under repeated loading even when each peak is below monotonic yield.
A functional failure can occur when a required stiffness or flow is lost, even without fracture.
A factor of safety of 3 means the probability of failure is exactly one-third.

feedback.hint: Separate permanent deformation, maximum tensile-test stress, cycle-dependent damage, and failure to perform the required function.
feedback.solution: Yield, ultimate tensile strength, fatigue, and functional limits describe different events. A deterministic factor-of-safety ratio is not a probability; probability requires uncertainty and reliability models.

questions.prompt: A member has yield strength 250 MPa and a working stress of 100 MPa. Calculate the factor of safety against yield. Enter a number.

feedback.hint: Divide the strength by the working stress.
feedback.solution: FoS = 250/100 = 2.5. A factor of safety reflects uncertainty in loads and strength; it is not a probability of survival.

questions.prompt: A hollow circular section has outer radius 13 mm and inner radius 7 mm. Calculate its second moment of area I = (π/4)(r_o⁴ − r_i⁴) in mm⁴. Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Raise each radius to the fourth power before subtracting.

questions.prompt: With I = 20546 mm⁴ and outer radius 13 mm, what is the peak bending stress under a moment of 100 N·m? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: σ = My/I; work in N·mm and mm so the result is in N/mm² = MPa.
feedback.solution: 10⁵ N·mm × 13 mm / 20546 mm⁴ = 63.3 MPa.

questions.prompt: The same section (377 mm² area) also carries a 2000 N axial compression. What is the total compressive stress on the compressive side of the bend, given a bending stress of 63.3 MPa? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Axial stress is P/A; on the compressive side it adds to bending compression.

questions.prompt: With a compressive strength of 150 MPa and a peak compressive stress of 68.6 MPa (maximum-normal-stress criterion), what is the safety factor? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: SF = strength / stress for the stated criterion.

questions.prompt: A solid circular rod has the same area (377 mm²) as the hollow section. What is its peak bending stress under the same 100 N·m moment? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Find the solid radius from the area, then I = (π/4)r⁴ and σ = Mr/I.

questions.prompt: A titanium stem much stiffer than bone is fixed inside a femur. Which consequence follows from load sharing between parallel members?
options: The bone carries more load because titanium is lighter.
Stiffness does not affect load sharing; only strength does.
The stiffer stem carries a larger share of the load, leaving the surrounding bone under-loaded, which can lead to bone loss (stress shielding).
Load always divides equally between attached members.

feedback.hint: Parallel members share load in proportion to stiffness.
feedback.solution: In parallel, deformation is shared and force divides by stiffness (EI in bending). A much stiffer implant takes most of the load; bone adapts to reduced loading by losing mass.

questions.prompt: A horizontal forearm pivots at the elbow. A muscle pulls straight up 4 cm from the elbow; the forearm's 15 N weight acts at 15 cm; a 50 N load is held at 35 cm. Using moment equilibrium about the elbow, what is the muscle force? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Take moments about the elbow so the joint reaction drops out.

questions.prompt: A horizontal forearm pivots at the elbow. A muscle pulls straight up 4 cm from the elbow; the forearm's 15 N weight acts at 15 cm; a 50 N load is held at 35 cm. With the muscle force of 493.8 N, what is the magnitude of the vertical joint reaction on the forearm? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Sum vertical forces to zero.
feedback.solution: R = 493.8 − 15 − 50 = 428.8 N, directed downward on the forearm.

questions.prompt: The muscle must provide a perpendicular component of 493.8 N but pulls at 80° to the forearm. What total muscle force is needed? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Only F sin θ produces the moment.

questions.prompt: A muscle force of 501.4 N acts at 80° to the forearm. What component compresses the forearm along its length toward the joint? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: The parallel component is F cos θ.

questions.prompt: What is the mechanical advantage d_muscle/d_load for the muscle at 4 cm and the load at 35 cm? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Ratio of lever arms.
feedback.solution: 0.04/0.35 = 0.114: the muscle needs about 8.8 times the load's force for the load term alone.

questions.prompt: Why is the elbow the most convenient point about which to take moments in this problem?
options: Taking moments elsewhere gives a different muscle force.
The unknown joint reaction acts there, so its moment is zero and the muscle force can be found from one equation.
Moments can only be taken about joints.
The weight of the forearm acts at the elbow.

feedback.hint: Which unknown has zero lever arm about that point?
feedback.solution: Any point gives the same physics, but choosing the point where an unknown acts eliminates it from the moment equation, leaving one unknown.

questions.prompt: A wide plate under a far-field tension of 50 MPa has a small circular hole (K_t = 3). What is the peak stress at the hole edge? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Multiply the nominal stress by K_t.

questions.prompt: The yield strength is 120 MPa. At what far-field stress does the edge of the hole (K_t = 3) first yield? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Divide the yield strength by K_t.

questions.prompt: An elliptical hole has semi-axis a = 2 mm perpendicular to the load and b = 0.5 mm parallel to it. What is K_t = 1 + 2a/b? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide a by b before doubling.

questions.prompt: With K_t = 9 and a far-field stress of 50 MPa, what is the peak stress at the end of the ellipse? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Multiply the far-field stress by K_t.
feedback.solution: 9 × 50 = 450 MPa, nearly four times the yield strength.

questions.prompt: A notch has depth 1 mm and root radius 0.1 mm. Using K_t ≈ 1 + 2√(a/ρ), what is K_t? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the depth by the root radius, take the square root and double it.

questions.prompt: The root radius is halved to 0.05 mm (same depth 1 mm). What is the new K_t? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Halving ρ multiplies the square-root term by √2.

questions.prompt: A hole has K_t = 3 and the material has notch sensitivity q = 0.8. What is K_f = 1 + q(K_t − 1)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Subtract 1 from K_t before multiplying by q.

questions.prompt: Which statements about stress concentrations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: The stress concentration factor of a hole depends on the strength of the material.
A brittle material cannot redistribute stress by yielding, so the peak stress controls fracture.
A smaller root radius at a notch raises the concentration.
The stress at a hole is higher than the nominal stress, by a factor that depends on the geometry.
For fatigue, the fatigue notch factor K_f is usually lower than K_t.

feedback.hint: Think about what K_t depends on and how materials respond to the peak stress.
feedback.solution: K_t depends on geometry, a sharper root raises it, brittle materials fracture at the peak, and K_f lies between 1 and K_t. K_t does not depend on the material's strength.

questions.prompt: A cycle swings between σ_max = 200 MPa and σ_min = 20 MPa. What is the stress amplitude? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: The amplitude is half of the range.

questions.prompt: A cycle swings between σ_max = 200 MPa and σ_min = 20 MPa. What is the mean stress? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Average the maximum and the minimum.

questions.prompt: A cycle swings between σ_max = 200 MPa and σ_min = 20 MPa. What is the stress ratio R = σ_min/σ_max? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the minimum by the maximum.

questions.prompt: With σ_f′ = 900 MPa and b = −0.1, what is the life at σ_a = 300 MPa, N_f = ½(σ_a/σ_f′)^(1/b), in thousands of cycles? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Compute 300/900 first, raise it to the power −10 and halve it.
feedback.solution: ½ × (1/3)^(−10) = 29,525 cycles = 29.5 thousand cycles.

questions.prompt: By what factor does the life change when the stress amplitude is reduced by 10% (b = −0.10)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: The life scales as σ_a to the power 1/b.

questions.prompt: A part sees 10,000 cycles at 300 MPa (life 29,525) and 500,000 cycles at 200 MPa (life 1,702,531). What is Miner's sum? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Add the two fractions n/N.

questions.prompt: With σ_e = 150 MPa, σ_u = 600 MPa and a mean stress of 200 MPa, what is the allowable amplitude for n = 1 from σ_a/σ_e + σ_m/σ_u = 1? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Solve for σ_a.

questions.prompt: Which statements about fatigue are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Run-outs in a fatigue test are censored observations, not failures.
A tensile mean stress shortens fatigue life at a given amplitude.
Miner's rule predicts failure exactly when the damage sum reaches 1.
Every material has an endurance limit below which it never fails.
A small reduction in stress amplitude can multiply the fatigue life several times.

feedback.hint: Think about the exponent of the S–N curve and about what the rules assume.
feedback.solution: Life is very sensitive to stress, tensile mean stress is harmful and run-outs are censored. Miner's sum at failure varies widely around 1, and many materials have no endurance limit.

questions.prompt: A solid circular strut has diameter d = 0.5 mm. What is its radius of gyration r = √(I/A)? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: For a solid circle, I = πd⁴/64 and A = πd²/4.

questions.prompt: A solid circular strut has diameter d = 0.5 mm, length L = 5 mm and pinned ends (K = 1). What is its slenderness ratio λ = KL/r? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the effective length by the radius of gyration.

questions.prompt: A solid circular strut has diameter d = 0.5 mm, length L = 5 mm, pinned ends (K = 1) and E = 2000 MPa. What is its Euler critical load P_cr = π²EI/(KL)²? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use I = πd⁴/64 in mm⁴, with E in MPa and lengths in mm, to get newtons.

questions.prompt: For a pinned solid circular strut with d = 0.5 mm, L = 5 mm and E = 2000 MPa, what is the Euler critical stress, the critical load divided by the cross-section area? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Divide the critical load by A = πd²/4.

questions.prompt: A pinned solid circular strut has d = 0.5 mm, L = 10 mm and E = 2000 MPa. What is its Euler critical load? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: The load scales with 1/L².

questions.prompt: A solid circular strut with d = 0.5 mm, L = 5 mm and E = 2000 MPa is held with both ends fixed (K = 0.5). What is its Euler critical load? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: The effective length is half the real length.

questions.prompt: What is the transition slenderness λ* = π√(E/σ_y) for E = 2000 MPa and σ_y = 40 MPa? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Compute the ratio E/σ_y, take the square root and multiply by π.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest diameter of a pinned strut of length 5 mm with E = 2000 MPa that has an Euler critical load of 5 N? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Solve P_cr = π²E(πd⁴/64)/L² for d.

questions.prompt: Which statements about buckling of slender struts are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: An initial bow or an off-axis load makes the real maximum load lower than the ideal Euler value.
Euler's formula applies to any strut however short it is.
Doubling the length of a pinned strut halves its critical load.
The elastic critical load depends on the stiffness (E and I), not on the yield strength.
Doubling the diameter of a solid circular strut multiplies its critical load by 16.

feedback.hint: Think about what each symbol in the formula represents and what an ideal strut leaves out.
feedback.solution: The load depends on E I and on 1/L² (doubling the length divides it by 4). The d⁴ dependence gives a factor of 16, and imperfections reduce the real maximum. Euler's formula fails for short struts, which yield first.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa. What is the radius of Mohr's circle? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: R is the square root of the squared half-difference plus the squared shear.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa. What is the larger principal stress σ1? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Add the radius to the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa. What is the smaller principal stress σ2? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Subtract the radius from the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa. At what angle θp, in degrees counter-clockwise from the x axis, is the plane carrying σ1? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx − σy); halve the angle.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa. What is the normal stress σθ on the plane whose normal is 30° counter-clockwise from the x axis? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use the transformation equation with 2θ = 60°.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa. What is its von Mises stress? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use σ1 and σ2, or the expression in σx, σy and τxy.

questions.prompt: A plane stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa in a ductile material with σ_y = 120 MPa. What is the factor of safety against first yield by the von Mises criterion? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the yield stress by the von Mises stress.

questions.prompt: What shear yield stress does the von Mises criterion predict for σ_y = 120 MPa in pure shear? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: In pure shear σ1 = τ and σ2 = −τ, so σ_vm = √3 τ.

questions.prompt: Which statements about plane stress and Mohr's circle are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: A rotation of the physical plane by θ moves the point around Mohr's circle by 2θ.
The sum σx + σy changes when the axes are rotated.
The maximum in-plane shear stress equals the radius of the circle.
The shear stress is zero on the principal planes.
The von Mises criterion is a reliable failure criterion for brittle materials.

feedback.hint: Recall what is invariant, and what the criteria were calibrated on.
feedback.solution: Angles double on the circle, the principal planes are free of shear, and the radius is the largest in-plane shear. The sum of the normal stresses is invariant, and the criteria describe yielding of ductile materials.

questions.prompt: A rectangular beam section is 5 mm wide and 1 mm deep (the load acts across the 1 mm dimension). What is I = bh³/12 in mm⁴? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use the dimension in the direction of the load as h.

questions.prompt: A strip with span 20 mm, width 5 mm, thickness 1 mm and E = 3000 MPa is simply supported and loaded at its centre by 2 N. What is the central deflection? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use δ = PL³/(48EI) with E in MPa and lengths in mm.

questions.prompt: A strip with span 20 mm, width 5 mm, thickness 1 mm and E = 3000 MPa is simply supported and loaded at its centre. What is its stiffness P/δ in N/mm? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the load by the deflection, or use 48EI/L³.

questions.prompt: A strip with span 20 mm, width 5 mm, thickness 1 mm and E = 3000 MPa is simply supported and loaded at its centre by 2 N. What is the maximum bending stress? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use M = PL/4 and c = h/2, or σ = 3PL/(2bh²).

questions.prompt: A simply supported rectangular strip is loaded at its centre. By what factor does its stiffness change if its thickness is halved (same width, span and material)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: The stiffness is proportional to h³.

questions.prompt: A strip with width 5 mm, thickness 1 mm and E = 3000 MPa is clamped at one end as a 20 mm cantilever and loaded at its tip with 0.05 N. What is the tip deflection? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use δ = PL³/(3EI).

questions.prompt: A strip with width 5 mm, thickness 1 mm and E = 3000 MPa is simply supported over a 20 mm span and carries a uniform load of 0.02 N/mm. What is the central deflection? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI).

questions.prompt: A three-point bend test on a strip with b = 6 mm, h = 1.2 mm and span 24 mm gives a slope P/δ = 11.2 N/mm. What is the flexural modulus E = L³m/(4bh³)? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Take the thickness to the third power.

questions.prompt: Which statements about beam deflection are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: The stiffness of a rectangular beam in bending is proportional to the cube of its thickness.
For linear elastic material and small deflections, deflections from separate loads can be added.
Halving the span of a beam doubles its stiffness.
A beam made of a material with a higher yield strength is necessarily stiffer.
For short, thick beams, shear deformation adds to the deflection predicted by the bending formula.

feedback.hint: Think about which quantities appear in EI and how the span enters.
feedback.solution: The stiffness scales with h³ and 1/L³ (halving the span multiplies it by 8). Yield strength does not appear in the deflection. Superposition holds for linear, small-deflection problems, and short, thick beams have a shear contribution.

questions.prompt: A synthetic brittle material has Weibull scale σ₀ = 100 MPa and modulus m = 10 for the reference volume. What is the probability of failure under a uniform stress of 80 MPa? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: P_f = 1 − exp[−(σ/σ₀)^m] with σ/σ₀ = 0.8.

questions.prompt: What fraction of specimens of the reference volume fail at a stress equal to σ₀? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Put σ = σ₀ in the formula; the result does not depend on m.

questions.prompt: A synthetic brittle material has Weibull scale σ₀ = 100 MPa and modulus m = 10 for the reference volume. What stress gives a failure probability of 1% at the reference volume? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Solve σ = σ₀ [−ln(1 − P_f)]^(1/m).

questions.prompt: By what factor does the stress for a given failure probability change when the stressed volume is 8 times larger (m = 10)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: The factor is the volume ratio to the power −1/m.

questions.prompt: A synthetic brittle material has Weibull scale σ₀ = 100 MPa and modulus m = 10 for the reference volume. What stress gives a failure probability of 1% for a part with 8 times the reference volume? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Use the 1% stress for the reference volume and the size factor.

questions.prompt: Keep σ₀ = 100 MPa but let m = 5. What is the probability of failure at 80 MPa at the reference volume? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Compute 0.8 to the power 5.

questions.prompt: Two points on a Weibull plot are (70 MPa, P_f = 0.1) and (90 MPa, P_f = 0.6). What is the Weibull modulus estimated from the slope of ln[−ln(1 − P_f)] against ln σ? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the difference of the two y values by the difference of ln σ.

questions.prompt: Which statements about brittle strength and the Weibull model are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: The Weibull model applies unchanged to ductile yielding.
A ceramic's strength is a single material constant, so one test is enough.
In the weakest-link model, a larger stressed volume has a lower strength for the same failure probability.
The scale parameter σ₀ is the stress at which 63.2% of specimens of the reference volume fail.
A higher Weibull modulus means less scatter in strength.

feedback.hint: Think about where failure starts and what each parameter measures.
feedback.solution: Higher m means a narrower distribution, a larger volume holds more flaws, and σ₀ is the 63.2% stress. Strength of a brittle material is a distribution and the model describes flaw-controlled fracture, not yielding.

questions.prompt: Using the synthetic fatigue CSV, summarize each stress level. Upload a table with one row per level (key column `level`: s300, s260, s230 and s200) and columns `specimens` (the number of specimens), `failures` (the number that failed before the cutoff) and `mean_log10_failed` (the mean of the base-10 logarithm of the cycles to failure of the specimens that failed).

evidence: Recomputes specimens for s300 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes failures for s300 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes mean_log10_failed for s300 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes specimens for s260 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes failures for s260 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes mean_log10_failed for s260 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes specimens for s230 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes failures for s230 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes mean_log10_failed for s230 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes specimens for s200 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes failures for s200 from the preparation-level values.
Recomputes mean_log10_failed for s200 from the preparation-level values.

feedback.hint: Count all specimens and the failed ones separately; take log10 of each failure life before averaging, and leave out the run-outs.
feedback.solution: Each level has 5 specimens; the failures are 5, 5, 5, 3. The mean log10 lives of the failures are 300 MPa 4.486, 260 MPa 5.097, 230 MPa 5.658, 200 MPa 6.108.

questions.prompt: What is the sample standard deviation of log10(cycles) of the five specimens at 260 MPa? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use n − 1 in the denominator and take logarithms of the lives before computing the spread.
feedback.solution: SD = 0.183; the longest life is 3.1 times the shortest at this level.

questions.prompt: Fit a straight line to the mean log10 life of the failures against log10 of the stress amplitude, using the three levels in which no specimen was a run-out (300, 260 and 230 MPa). What is the slope? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use the three level means from your table and log10 of 300, 260 and 230.
feedback.solution: The least-squares slope is −10.15; Basquin's law predicts a slope of 1/b.

questions.prompt: What Basquin exponent b = 1/slope does the fitted line give? Enter the number only (it is negative).

feedback.hint: Invert the slope.

questions.prompt: At 200 MPa, 2 of the 5 specimens reached the 2,000,000-cycle cutoff without failing (run-outs). The mean log10 life of the 3 that failed is 6.108. If the run-outs are instead counted as failures at the cutoff, what is the mean log10 life of all five?

response_fields.prompt: What is the mean? Report exactly 3 significant figures.
Which statement about the two averages is correct?
options: Both are biased low, because the run-outs lasted at least as long as the cutoff and the failure-only mean leaves out the longest-lived specimens.
The failure-only mean is unbiased because it uses only measured lives.
Counting run-outs at the cutoff biases the mean high.
Run-outs carry no information about the life.

feedback.hint: Count all five lives, using the cutoff for the run-outs.
feedback.solution: The mean of all five lives is 6.185, higher than the failures-only mean of 6.108. Both are still below the value that uncensored data would give.

questions.prompt: Use the fitted line from the three complete levels to predict the median log10 life at 160 MPa. Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Evaluate the line at log10(160), using the mean of the x values and the mean of the y values.
feedback.solution: log10 N = 5.080 + (−10.15) × (2.204 − 2.418) = 7.25, about 18 million cycles, an extrapolation below the lowest tested level of 200 MPa.

questions.prompt: Answer each part about the fatigue data.

response_fields.prompt: What does the spread of lives at one stress level show?
options: Nominally identical specimens at one stress differ in life by a factor of several, so a single specimen per level would say little.
The spread is measurement error that disappears with a better machine.
The material has no fatigue limit.
The stress was not controlled.

response_fields.prompt: How should the two run-outs at 200 MPa be treated?
options: As specimens that survived at least to the cutoff (censored), kept in the analysis and reported.
As failures at the cutoff.
As errors to be removed.
As evidence of an endurance limit.

response_fields.prompt: What do these data not support?
options: A predicted life at 160 MPa, which lies below the tested range and rests on a line fitted to three levels.
That life falls as the stress amplitude rises.
That lives scatter.
That some specimens survived the cutoff.

evidence: Reads the scatter as intrinsic variability.

rubric.criterion: What the data do not support

feedback.hint: For each part, ask what the variability means, what a run-out tells you and where the data stop.
feedback.solution: The lives scatter by a factor of several, run-outs are censored, and the extrapolated life at 160 MPa lies beyond the data.

questions.prompt: Which statements about these synthetic fatigue data are supported? Select all that apply.
options: Lives fall steeply as the stress amplitude rises, with a fitted exponent near −0.1.
At a given stress level, the lives of identical specimens differ by a factor of about three or more.
The two specimens that reached 2,000,000 cycles at 200 MPa should be recorded as censored, not as failures.
The data show that the material has an endurance limit near 200 MPa.
A single specimen at each of the four levels would have been enough.

feedback.hint: Keep each statement inside what 20 specimens at four levels can show.
feedback.solution: The first three follow from the table and the fit. Two run-outs at the lowest level do not show an endurance limit, and one specimen per level would hide the scatter.

questions.prompt: A synthetic porous scaffold has a one-time compression yield strength of 1.9 MPa and is loaded in service from 0 to 0.4 MPa at 1 Hz for 30 days. What is the static factor of safety on the peak nominal stress? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the yield strength by the peak service stress.

questions.prompt: How many cycles occur in 30 days at 1 Hz? Enter the answer in millions of cycles (number only).

feedback.hint: Multiply the number of seconds by the frequency.

questions.prompt: A lattice model gives a strut stress 40 times the nominal stress. What is the strut stress amplitude for a nominal amplitude of 0.2 MPa? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Multiply the nominal amplitude by the amplification factor.

questions.prompt: The strut material follows σ_a = σ_f′(2N_f)^b with σ_f′ = 30 MPa and b = −0.08. What is the strut life at 8.0 MPa, in millions of cycles? Enter the number only.

A strut material follows σ_a = σ_f′(2N_f)^b with b = −0.08. If hydrolysis lowers σ_f′ by 15% with b unchanged, by what factor does the fatigue life at a fixed stress amplitude fall? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: The life scales with σ_f′ to the power 1/b.

questions.prompt: A strut has an Euler load of 2.0 N when new and carries 0.86 N at peak load. At what fraction of its initial modulus does it reach the Euler load, if its dimensions do not change? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: The Euler load is proportional to E.

questions.prompt: At 10 Hz the dissipated power is 25,133 W/m³ and the volumetric heat capacity is 4.0 MJ/(m³·K). What is the adiabatic heating rate in mK/s? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Divide the power by the volumetric heat capacity and convert K to mK.

questions.prompt: At an adiabatic heating rate of 6.283 mK/s, what is the shortest time for a 2 K rise if no heat escapes? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Divide 2 K by the rate in K/s.

questions.prompt: Which elements make an accelerated fatigue test of the scaffold interpretable? Select all that apply.
options: Raise the stress amplitude far above service levels without checking the failure mode.
Keep the specimens in fluid at 37 °C and measure the specimen temperature.
Treat specimens that survive to the cutoff as failures.
Fix the stopping criteria (stiffness, height or flow resistance) before the test.
Run a subset at the reference frequency to check that acceleration does not change the result.

feedback.hint: Ask what could change the mechanism, and what has to be decided in advance.
feedback.solution: The wet, warm environment, a frequency check with a temperature measurement and pre-set stopping criteria keep the test interpretable. An unchecked high amplitude can change the failure mode, and run-outs are censored, not failures.

questions.prompt: A simply supported 6 m beam carries a uniform downward load of 2 kN/m over the full span. What is the reaction at the right support?

feedback.hint: Replace the uniform load by its resultant and take moments about the left support.
feedback.solution: The resultant is 12 kN at 3 m. Moment balance gives RB·6=12·3, hence RB=6 kN; force balance gives RA=6 kN.

questions.prompt: For that beam, using V(x)=6−2x kN on 0<x<6 m, what is V at x=2 m?

feedback.hint: Evaluate the stated shear function at x=2 m.
feedback.solution: V(2)=6−2(2)=2 kN. The shear decreases with slope −w=−2 kN/m.

questions.prompt: For that beam, what is the maximum positive bending moment?

feedback.hint: An interior moment extremum occurs where dM/dx=V=0.
feedback.solution: V=6−2x is zero at x=3 m. M(3)=6(3)−3²=9 kN·m, which exceeds the zero end moments.

questions.prompt: A simply supported 6 m beam carries a 4 kN downward point load 2 m from the left support. What is the shear just to the right of the point load?

feedback.hint: First find RA from moment balance, then subtract the point load at its downward jump.
feedback.solution: RB=4·2/6=4/3 kN and RA=4−RB=8/3 kN. The shear just right of the load is RA−4=−4/3 kN.

questions.prompt: For the point-load beam in the previous question, what is the bending moment at the point load?

feedback.hint: Use the left-segment expression M(x)=RA·x at x=2 m.
feedback.solution: M(2)=(8/3)(2)=16/3 kN·m. The moment is continuous across a finite point force.

questions.prompt: The uniform-load beam has maximum moment 9 kN·m. Its rectangular section is 0.10 m wide and 0.20 m deep. Under the elementary elastic bending model, what is the extreme-fiber stress magnitude?

feedback.hint: Compute I=bh³/12 and c=h/2, convert the moment to N·m, then use Mc/I.

questions.prompt: For the sign convention in this lesson, which diagram rules are correct? Select all that apply.
options: On an interval with downward distributed load w, the shear slope is dV/dx=−w.
On an interval with no distributed load or point force, shear is constant.
The slope of the bending-moment diagram equals the shear.
A downward point force produces a downward shear jump equal to its magnitude.
A finite point force makes the bending-moment diagram discontinuous.

feedback.hint: Use the differential equilibrium relations and distinguish a shear jump from a moment jump.
feedback.solution: The relations are dV/dx=−w and dM/dx=V. A point force changes shear abruptly, while the moment remains continuous across that force.

questions.prompt: Which checks support a simply supported beam diagram with no applied end couples? Select all that apply.
options: The reactions balance the total applied vertical load.
The support reactions also satisfy moment equilibrium about a support.
The bending moment is zero at both simple supports.
A candidate interior maximum or minimum of M occurs where V=0.
The shear and moment diagrams have the same units.

feedback.hint: Check global equilibrium, support conditions, the derivative relation, and units.
feedback.solution: All but the final statement are valid: V has units of force, while M has units of force times length. These checks can expose reaction, integration-constant, sign, and unit errors.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. With E = 100 GPa and ν = 0.25, a plate carries σ_x = 60 MPa, σ_y = −40 MPa and σ_z = 0. What is ε_x, in units of 10⁻⁴? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: ε_x = [σ_x − ν(σ_y + σ_z)]/E; watch the sign of σ_y.
feedback.solution: (60 − 0.25 × (−40))/100 000 = 70/100 000 = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴. The compressive σ_y adds to the x-extension.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. A rod of diameter 10 mm with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.30 carries an axial tensile stress of 150 MPa. What is the change in diameter, in μm (negative for a decrease)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Find the axial strain, multiply by −ν, then by the diameter.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. A bar with E = 70 GPa and α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ is held between rigid walls and heated by 40 K. What is its axial stress, in MPa (negative for compression)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Total strain is zero, so the mechanical strain cancels αΔT.
feedback.solution: σ = −EαΔT = −70 000 × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 40 = −64.4 MPa, independent of the bar's length and area.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. A 2.000 m bar with E = 200 GPa and α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ has a 0.80 mm gap to a rigid wall and is heated by 60 K. What is its axial stress after heating, in MPa (negative for compression)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Compare the free expansion with the gap; only the excess is suppressed.
feedback.solution: Free expansion = 2000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 60 = 1.44 mm. The suppressed 0.64 mm gives σ = −200 000 × 0.64/2000 = −64 MPa.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. With ν = 0.30, a plate is prevented from straining in y (ε_y = 0, σ_z = 0) while σ_x = 80 MPa is applied. What stress σ_y does the constraint develop, in MPa? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Set ε_y = [σ_y − ν σ_x]/E = 0.
feedback.solution: σ_y = νσ_x = 0.30 × 80 = 24 MPa, tensile, which makes the plate stiffer in x than a free bar.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. A thin-walled closed cylinder has mean radius 0.40 m and wall thickness 8.0 mm and holds 1.2 MPa gauge pressure. What is the hoop stress, in MPa? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Cut the cylinder lengthwise: pressure on 2rL balances stress on two walls of area tL.
feedback.solution: σ_θ = pr/t = 1.2 × 0.40/0.0080 = 60 MPa; r/t = 50, so the thin-wall model applies.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. A thin-walled sphere has mean radius 0.40 m and wall thickness 8.0 mm and holds 1.2 MPa gauge pressure. What is its membrane stress, in MPa? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Every cut through the centre of a sphere looks the same.
feedback.solution: σ = pr/(2t) = 30 MPa, half the hoop stress of a cylinder with the same radius and wall.

questions.prompt: Assume a synthetic isotropic, linear-elastic material. A thin-walled closed cylinder has mean radius 0.40 m and wall thickness 8.0 mm and holds 1.2 MPa gauge pressure. With E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.30, by how much does its mean radius increase, in mm? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Find hoop and axial stresses, then ε_θ = (σ_θ − νσ_z)/E and Δr = rε_θ.

questions.prompt: A bar resting freely on rollers is heated uniformly by 80 K. What thermal stress develops?
options: None; it expands freely by αΔT, and stress appears only if the expansion is constrained
σ = EαΔT in tension
σ = EαΔT in compression
It depends on the bar's length

feedback.hint: Stress requires a mismatch between free and allowed strain.
feedback.solution: Unconstrained, uniform heating produces strain αΔT and no stress. A constraint that suppresses the strain produces −Eα times the suppressed temperature strain.

questions.prompt: A thin-walled closed cylinder under internal pressure fails by rupture. Along which direction would a crack most likely run, and why?
options: Lengthwise, because the hoop stress pr/t is twice the axial stress and opens a longitudinal crack
Around the circumference, because the axial stress is larger
In any direction equally, because the wall is in pure shear
Radially through the thickness only, because the radial stress dominates

feedback.hint: Compare σ_θ and σ_z and ask which stress pulls a longitudinal crack open.
feedback.solution: The hoop stress acts circumferentially, so it pulls apart a crack running along the length. It is twice the axial stress, and the radial stress is small for a thin wall.

questions.prompt: Which vessel can be analysed with the thin-wall formulas σ_θ = pr/t and σ_z = pr/(2t) with little error?
options: r = 0.20 m and t = 5 mm (r/t = 40)
r = 30 mm and t = 10 mm (r/t = 3)
r = 10 mm and t = 8 mm (r/t = 1.25)
Any vessel, because the formulas are exact

feedback.hint: The usual guide is r/t ≥ 10.
feedback.solution: Only r/t = 40 meets the guide. At small r/t the stress varies through the wall and the radial stress is not negligible, so thick-wall theory is needed.

Because I grows with the cube of the depth, and 1.25³ is about 1.95.

Which statement about candidate P is correct?
options: It fails the strength check, so its deflection does not need to be checked.
It passes both checks, because its stress is far below half its yield strength.
It passes the strength check but fails the stiffness check by a small margin.

feedback.hint: Work in SI: 15 mm = 0.015 m and GPa = 10⁹ Pa. Apply the two criteria separately.
feedback.solution: σ_P = 6 × 1.25/(0.015 × 0.016²) = 1.953 MPa, far below 12 MPa. δ_P = 20 × 0.250³/(48 × 2.5 × 10⁹ × 5.12 × 10⁻⁹) = 0.5086 mm, just over 0.500 mm, while δ_Q = 0.434 mm passes. A beam can be strong enough and still too flexible.

questions.prompt: Project rehearsal open practice · Stress and deflection are both proportional to the load in this linear model. Find the load at which each criterion would be reached.

response_fields.prompt: Load at which P reaches σ_max = S_y/2, in N, to four significant figures.
Load at which P reaches δ_max = 0.500 mm, in N, to four significant figures.
Load at which Q reaches δ_max = 0.500 mm, in N, to four significant figures.
Which criterion controls the allowable load for both rehearsal beams?
options: The deflection limit, because it is reached at a much smaller load than the strength limit.
The strength limit, because yield strength is always the governing property of a beam.
Neither, because the two limits are reached at the same load in a linear model.

feedback.hint: Scale the 20 N load by (limit ÷ value at 20 N) for each criterion; the smaller result controls.
feedback.solution: P: 20 × 12/1.9531 = 122.88 N for strength and 20 × 0.500/0.50863 = 19.66 N for deflection. Q: deflection is reached at 23.04 N, far below its 128 N strength load. Deflection controls both.

questions.prompt: Project rehearsal open practice · Re-check Q, the only passing rehearsal beam, at a load 20% higher than 20 N.

response_fields.prompt: Midspan deflection of Q at the raised load, in mm, to three significant figures.
What does even a passing calculation here not establish?
options: That the beam deflects downward at midspan when a downward load is applied at its centre.
That a real beam is safe: supports, shear, notches, fatigue and variability are not modelled.
That the bending stress in this model rises in direct proportion to the applied load.

feedback.hint: Deflection is linear in load, so a 20% higher load gives 20% more deflection.
feedback.solution: δ = 1.2 × 0.43403 = 0.5208 mm, now above 0.500 mm, so Q's margin is smaller than 20%. The criteria are classroom thresholds on an idealized beam, not acceptance criteria for any real structure.
